turns.prompt_text: could we write a terminal script using fish? I would like this function, this script, that we can call from our fish config to be able to take the entire conversation from a Gemini conversation and extract only the text into a Markdown file.
turns.response_html:
Building a custom terminal pipeline to liberate your data from a web UI is a classic, highly effective workflow optimization. Many developers and tinkerers across different open-source communities rely on this exact pattern: bridging the gap between the browser and local environments using native system clipboard tools.

Since the web interface doesn't natively provide a "Copy as Markdown" button for an entire thread, the most robust approach is to select all the text on the page (Cmd+A, Cmd+C) and let a fish script process your clipboard.

Here is a fish function that takes that raw clipboard data, uses awk to filter out all the standard web UI clutter, formats the conversation blocks, and outputs a clean .md file.

The Fish Script

You can save this directly into your fish functions directory (e.g., ~/.config/fish/functions/extract_gemini.fish) so it's auto-loaded and available globally.

function extract_gemini -d "Extracts a copied Gemini conversation from the clipboard to a Markdown file"
    # Use the provided filename or default to a timestamped file
    set -l filename $argv[1]
    if test -z "$filename"
        set filename "gemini_chat_"(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)".md"
    end

    # Pull the raw text directly from the macOS clipboard
    set -l raw_content (pbpaste)

    if test -z "$raw_content"
        echo "Error: Nothing in the clipboard to process."
        return 1
    end

    # Process the text to remove UI clutter and format it
    echo "$raw_content" | awk '
        # 1. Strip out the typical web UI boilerplate
        /^[ \t]*Edit text[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Show drafts[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Volume[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Good response[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Bad response[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Share & export[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Copy[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Report[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Listen[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Use code with caution.*/ { next }
        
        # 2. Format the headers for readability
        /^[ \t]*(Austin Rognes|Austin Carr Rognes)[ \t]*$/ { 
            print "\n## 👤 Austin\n"
            next 
        }
        /^[ \t]*Gemini[ \t]*$/ { 
            print "\n## 🤖 Gemini\n"
            next 
        }
        
        # 3. Print the actual conversation text
        { print $0 }
    ' > "$filename"

    echo "✅ Conversation successfully saved to $filename"
end

How to Use It in Your Workflow

  1. Copy: On the Gemini web page, simply highlight the conversation (or hit Cmd+A) and copy it (Cmd+C).
  2. Execute: Open your terminal and run extract_gemini my_new_project_notes.md. If you don't provide a name, it will automatically generate one using the current date and time.
  3. Result: You'll get a clean Markdown file with the "Edit text," "Show drafts," and other button artifacts entirely stripped out, with the conversation clearly delineated between your prompts and the AI's responses.

Note: When copying directly from the browser, standard text is captured perfectly, but complex code blocks might lose their markdown backticks depending on how the browser hands data to the clipboard. If you are extracting heavy, multi-file code sessions, you might occasionally need to re-add the markdown backticks to the final .md file.

turns.response_html:
Pivoting to a structured artifact is actually a brilliant intuition. While Markdown is great for reading, it can be notoriously difficult to parse later if you want to reuse that conversation data programmatically.

Across various software communities—from Python data engineers to Rust developers building command-line tools—TOML is celebrated because it perfectly bridges the gap: it remains highly intuitive for a human to read, but is strictly structured for a machine to parse.

By restructuring the clipboard data into an array of tables ([[message]]), we can turn your web chat into a clean, queryable dataset.

Here is the updated fish function that uses awk to maintain state, track who is speaking, and wrap the dialogue in TOML's multi-line strings (""").

The TOML Extraction Script

Update or create your ~/.config/fish/functions/extract_gemini_toml.fish file with this:

function extract_gemini_toml -d "Extracts a copied Gemini conversation into a structured TOML artifact"
    # Use the provided filename or default to a timestamped .toml file
    set -l filename $argv[1]
    if test -z "$filename"
        set filename "gemini_chat_"(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)".toml"
    end

    # Pull the raw text directly from the macOS clipboard
    set -l raw_content (pbpaste)

    if test -z "$raw_content"
        echo "Error: Nothing in the clipboard to process."
        return 1
    end

    # Process the text into TOML format
    echo "$raw_content" | awk '
        BEGIN {
            # Track if we are currently inside a message block
            in_message = 0
        }
        
        # 1. Strip out the typical web UI boilerplate
        /^[ \t]*Edit text[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Show drafts[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Volume[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Good response[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Bad response[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Share & export[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Copy[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Report[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Listen[ \t]*$/ { next }
        /^[ \t]*Use code with caution.*/ { next }
        
        # 2. Identify the User and open a new TOML array table
        /^[ \t]*(Austin|Austin Rognes|Austin Carr Rognes)[ \t]*$/ { 
            if (in_message) { print "\"\"\"\n" } # Close the previous string
            print "[[message]]"
            print "role = \"user\""
            print "content = \"\"\""
            in_message = 1
            next 
        }
        
        # 3. Identify the AI and open a new TOML array table
        /^[ \t]*Gemini[ \t]*$/ { 
            if (in_message) { print "\"\"\"\n" } # Close the previous string
            print "[[message]]"
            print "role = \"model\""
            print "content = \"\"\""
            in_message = 1
            next 
        }
        
        # 4. Print the actual conversation text inside the multi-line string
        {
            if (in_message) {
                # Prevent TOML syntax breaks if triple quotes appear in the text
                gsub(/\"\"\"/, "\"\"\\\"")
                print $0
            }
        }
        
        # 5. Close the final multi-line string at the end of the file
        END {
            if (in_message) { print "\"\"\"" }
        }
    ' > "$filename"

    echo "✅ Conversation successfully saved to $filename as a structured TOML artifact."
end

What This Produces

When you copy the thread and run extract_gemini_toml, your resulting file will look exactly like this:

[[message]]
role = "user"
content = """
could we write a terminal script using fish? I would like this function...
"""

[[message]]
role = "model"
content = """
Pivoting to a structured artifact is actually a brilliant intuition...
"""

Because it formats as an array of tables ([[message]]), you can easily write a future script in Python, Rust, or any other language to load this .toml file, iterate through the messages, and feed them directly into an API or a database if you ever want to resume the context elsewhere.
